title: Freelancing Fundamentals: Package, Price and Deliver Paid Work
subtitle: Turn one skill you already have into a clearly priced freelance service, win your first clients and deliver paid work professionally.
description: A practical course for women ready to earn from a skill such as writing, design, virtual assistance, translation or bookkeeping support. You will choose a service with real demand, calculate prices that cover your time, pitch and agree jobs in writing, deliver and invoice professionally, and finish with a real outreach record and a 90-day plan.
outcomes: Choose one freelance service using demand evidence and describe it in a one-sentence offer line
Calculate a minimum hourly rate and build three priced packages, allowing for platform fees
Write personal pitches, track an outreach funnel and agree each job with a written scope and deposit
Deliver on time, invoice correctly, chase late payments and avoid common freelance scams
Track effective hourly rate, average job value and repeat clients, and plan the next 90 days

Reliable data with a backup SIM or network

modules.title: Foundations: choosing a freelance service you can sell
modules.overview: Understand how freelancing really works as a small business, pick one service with real demand, and set up the money, tools and safety habits you need before your first client.

lessons.title: How freelancing works: the client cycle and where your time goes
objectives: Explain the difference between freelancing, employment and selling products
Describe the six stages of the freelance client cycle
Calculate how many of your working hours can realistically be paid
Decide whether freelancing fits your current responsibilities

blocks.text: A **freelancer** is a self-employed person who sells a service to several clients, one project or one month at a time. There is no employer paying a salary, no fixed office and no one handing out work. You are a one-person business: you find the client, agree the job, do it, send the bill and make sure you are paid. That is why this course treats freelancing as a business skill, not only a talent.

Freelancing is different from selling products. A trader buys stock and sells it again. A freelancer sells **time, skill and results**: a written article, a cleaned-up spreadsheet, a month of social media posts, a translated document, a set of bookkeeping records. You cannot store a service on a shelf, so every naira you earn is tied to work you actually deliver.

blocks.name: freelancer
blocks.alt: A woman working on a laptop at a desk
blocks.caption: A freelancer runs a one-person service business from wherever she has a device and a connection.

blocks.text: Common digital freelance services
Most online freelance work falls into a few families. You do not need to be an expert in all of them. You need one service that you can do well and explain clearly.

head: Service family
Typical deliverable
Typical clients
rows: Blog articles, product descriptions, CVs, proofreading
Small online shops, schools, NGOs, job seekers
Inbox and calendar management, data entry, customer replies
Monthly content calendar, designed posts, replies to comments
Monthly sales and expense records in a spreadsheet

blocks.text: The freelance client cycle

Every freelance job, small or large, passes through the same six stages. Beginners often focus only on stage four, doing the work, and are surprised when the money does not come. Each stage needs its own skill, and this course has a lesson for each one.

blocks.title: The freelance client cycle
items: Find the client
Pitch and discuss
Agree scope and price
Deliver the work
Invoice and get paid
Keep and get referrals
blocks.caption: Each finished job feeds the next one through repeat work and referrals, so the cycle gets easier the longer you keep it turning.

items: **Find:** let the right people know your service exists (your network, platforms, direct messages).
**Pitch:** reply to a need with a short, specific message and a sample.
**Agree:** put the scope, deadline, price and payment terms in writing before you start.
**Deliver:** do the work to the agreed standard, on time, with clear updates.
**Get paid:** send a proper invoice and collect a deposit or full payment.
**Keep:** ask for feedback and a testimonial, and offer the next piece of work.

blocks.text: Billable and non-billable hours

A **billable hour** is an hour you spend doing work a client pays for. A **non-billable hour** is business work nobody pays you for directly: looking for clients, writing pitches, answering enquiries that go nowhere, sending invoices, learning, and fixing your own laptop. Many experienced freelancers find that a large share of their week, often a quarter to a half, is non-billable, especially in the first year. If you price your work as though every hour is paid, you will earn far less than you planned.

blocks.title: Worked example: how many hours can actually earn money?
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Ibadan has two school-age children. She can work from 9 am to 2 pm on weekdays and for two hours on Saturday.
steps: Weekday hours: 5 hours x 5 days = 25 hours. Saturday adds 2 hours, so 27 working hours a week.
She sets aside 1 hour a day on weekdays for finding clients and admin: 5 hours a week.
She allows another 4 hours a week for unpaid revisions, calls and learning.
Billable hours left: 27 minus 5 minus 4 = 18 hours a week.
Over a month of about 4 weeks: 18 x 4 = 72 billable hours, not 108.
blocks.result: Amaka will plan her income around 72 paid hours a month. In Module 2 she will use this number to work out her minimum rate, instead of guessing.

blocks.title: Freelancing is not passive income
blocks.text: Your income stops when you stop working, and there is no paid leave or pension unless you create it yourself. The upside is control: you choose your clients, your hours and your prices, and you can raise them as your skill and reputation grow.
Is this the right time for you?

Freelancing suits women who need flexible hours, have a skill other people struggle with, and can tolerate months when income is uneven. It is harder if you need a fixed amount every month starting next week, because most new freelancers take weeks or months to land steady clients. Many women start freelancing alongside a job, trade or studies, then grow it gradually. That is a sensible path, not a weakness.

takeaways: Freelancing is running a one-person service business, not just having a skill.
Every job passes through six stages: find, pitch, agree, deliver, get paid, keep.
Only part of your working time is billable, so plan income on billable hours.
Starting alongside other income is a realistic and common route.

activity.title: Map your real working week
steps: Write down every block of time you could work each day for one normal week.
Add the hours to get your total working hours.
Subtract at least 20 percent for finding clients and admin.
Multiply the billable hours left by 4 to get your monthly billable hours.
Note which of the six client-cycle stages feels hardest for you today.
activity.evidence: A one-page note or photo of your weekly time plan showing total hours, billable hours and your hardest stage.

lessons.title: Choosing one service with real demand and writing your offer line
objectives: List your skills and test which ones people actually pay for
Use evidence, not guesswork, to judge demand for a service
Write a one-sentence offer line that names a client, a result and a service
Narrow a broad skill into a specific, sellable service

blocks.text: The most common beginner mistake is offering everything: "I do writing, design, typing, social media, anything you need." It feels safer, but clients hire people who look like a clear answer to one problem. A business owner with a messy Instagram page wants a social media manager, not someone who might be able to help with it among ten other things. Your first job in freelancing is to choose **one service** and make it easy to understand.
Step 1: list what you can already do

Start with skills you have used for real, at work, in church or community groups, in school or for family. Write each as a task, not a quality. "Organised" is a quality. "Keeps a monthly expense spreadsheet for our cooperative" is a task someone could pay for.
Step 2: test demand with evidence
Demand means people are already paying, or actively asking, for this service. You can find evidence in about an hour with your phone:

items: **Job and gig sites:** search the service on Upwork, Fiverr, LinkedIn Jobs or Jobberman and note how many recent posts or sellers you see.
**Local businesses:** look at five businesses near you or on Instagram. Is their menu badly designed, their page silent for months, their price list unclear?
**Your network:** ask ten people who run businesses: "Do you pay anyone for this, or wish you could?"
**WhatsApp and Facebook groups:** search business groups you already belong to for requests like "I need someone to..."

blocks.title: Many sellers is a good sign
blocks.text: If you find many freelancers already offering a service, that usually proves people buy it. It means you must be more specific, not that you should give up. No sellers at all can mean no buyers.
Step 3: score your options
Compare each skill on two things: how strong you are at it today, and how much evidence of demand you found. The matrix below shows what to do with each combination.

blocks.title: Skill strength and demand
items: Practise, then sell
Sell this first
Drop for now
Keep as a hobby
blocks.caption: Start with the service in the top-right box: a skill you are good at that people already pay for.

blocks.text: Read the matrix like this. High demand but weak skill (top left): practise for a few weeks before selling. High demand and strong skill (top right): this is your first service. Low demand and weak skill (bottom left): drop it for now. Strong skill but little demand (bottom right): enjoy it, but do not build your income plan on it.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing between three skills
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in Kaduna can type fast, designs flyers for her church in Canva, and speaks Hausa and English fluently.
steps: Typing: she finds many data-entry gigs online, but most pay very little and attract scams. Skill high, demand high but low-paying. She keeps it as a backup.
Flyer design: she counts 14 event and church pages in her city with poor flyers and three people in her network say they pay a designer. Skill medium, demand high.
Hausa to English translation: she finds requests from NGOs and researchers in two LinkedIn searches and one Upwork search. Skill high, demand medium to high, and fewer competitors.
She scores each from 1 to 5 on skill and demand: typing 5 and 2 (because of the low pay), design 3 and 4, translation 5 and 4.
blocks.result: Translation scores highest (9 out of 10), so Hausa to English translation becomes her first service. She keeps practising design to add later.

blocks.name: target-audience
blocks.alt: A person pointing at a chosen group of customers
blocks.caption: A clear offer is aimed at one specific group of clients with a problem you can solve.

blocks.text: Step 4: write your offer line

An **offer line** is one sentence that tells a stranger exactly what you do. Use this pattern: **I help [specific client] get [result they want] by [your service].** It names who it is for, why they would care, and what you actually do.

head: Too broad
Specific offer line
rows: I help small online fashion shops sell more by writing clear product descriptions for their catalogue.
I help busy coaches get back about 5 hours a week by managing their inbox and booking calendar.
I help NGOs and researchers reach Hausa-speaking communities by translating surveys and leaflets from English.
I help restaurants in Port Harcourt stay visible by planning and posting 12 Instagram posts a month.

blocks.text: Notice that the specific lines also hint at the deliverable (product descriptions, 12 posts a month), which makes pricing easier later. Avoid promising results you cannot control, such as "double your sales". You can promise the work and a reasonable benefit, not the client's profit.

blocks.title: Specific is not permanent
blocks.text: Choosing one service now does not lock you in forever. Freelancers often start narrow, build a reputation, and then add related services that the same clients ask for. Narrow first makes the first clients come faster.
If you also want to build an online portfolio, the WODDI Institute course on online portfolio building goes deeper into showing your work. Here we focus on choosing and selling the service itself.

takeaways: Clients hire a clear answer to one problem, so choose one service first.
Demand is proven by evidence: job posts, requests and people already paying.
Sell first where your skill is strong and demand is clear.
Your offer line names the client, the result and the service.

activity.title: Test three skills and write your offer line
steps: Write three skills as specific tasks someone could pay for.
Spend 20 minutes per skill gathering demand evidence from at least two sources.
Score each skill from 1 to 5 on strength and on demand.
Choose the top-scoring skill and write your offer line using the pattern.
Read your offer line to one person and ask them to repeat back what you do.
activity.evidence: A short table of your three skills with scores and evidence notes, plus your final offer line.

lessons.title: Your setup: tools, payment channels, money buffer and scam safety
objectives: Check that your device, connection and tools are ready for client work
Choose safe payment channels for local and international clients
Calculate a money buffer for months when income is uneven
Recognise and refuse the most common freelance scams

blocks.text: Before you look for clients, make sure you can actually do the work, get paid and stay safe. A client who waits two days because your data ran out, or a payment that never arrives because you used an unsafe channel, can undo weeks of effort. This lesson is your readiness checklist.
Tools and connection

Much freelance work can start on a smartphone: writing in Google Docs, designing in Canva, managing WhatsApp Business, keeping records in Google Sheets. Some services, such as long documents, spreadsheets or design files for print, are much easier on a laptop. Be honest about what your service needs. You also need a reliable connection: keep a backup, such as a second SIM on a different network, and know where you can go if power or data fails on a deadline day.

items: **A professional email address:** firstname.lastname or a business name on Gmail, not a nickname.
**Cloud storage:** Google Drive or similar, so work is not lost if your phone is stolen or damaged.
**A calendar:** Google Calendar for deadlines and client calls, with reminders switched on.
**WhatsApp Business:** a separate business profile with your offer line and working hours.
**Two-step verification** switched on for email and WhatsApp, so a stolen password is not enough to take over your accounts.

blocks.name: security-on
blocks.alt: A person switching on account security on a device
blocks.caption: Two-step verification on your email and WhatsApp protects your client files and your income.

blocks.text: Getting paid safely

head: Client type
Common payment channels
Points to check
rows: Bank transfer, Opay, Moniepoint, Paystack payment link
Confirm money has arrived in your app or bank statement, not from a screenshot
Domiciliary (foreign currency) bank account, Payoneer and similar services
Fees and exchange rates vary, so compare them before you quote
Platform pays you, then you withdraw to bank or Payoneer
Platforms charge service and withdrawal fees; read the current fee page

blocks.title: Screenshots are not payment
blocks.text: Fake transfer alerts and edited screenshots are common. Only start or release work when the money shows in your own banking app or statement.
Your money buffer

New freelancers usually have uneven months. A **buffer** is savings that cover your essential costs while you build clients, so you are not forced to accept bad jobs out of panic. A common rule of thumb is to aim for about three months of essential costs. If you cannot save that yet, keep your current income source while you start, and grow the buffer from your first freelance earnings.

blocks.title: Worked example: working out a buffer
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Lagos plans to freelance as a virtual assistant while keeping her part-time shop job for now. All figures are approximate.
steps: Her essential monthly costs: rent share 60,000 naira, food 70,000, transport 25,000, data and airtime 15,000, children's school costs averaged per month 30,000. Total: 200,000 naira.
Three months of essentials: 200,000 x 3 = 600,000 naira.
Her shop job pays enough to cover 150,000 a month, leaving a gap of 50,000 a month.
Buffer for her actual gap over three months: 50,000 x 3 = 150,000 naira.
She plans to save 25 percent of every freelance payment until the 150,000 buffer is complete.
blocks.result: Because she keeps her job, Chioma needs a 150,000 naira buffer, not 600,000. She will consider leaving the job only when freelance income has covered the gap for several months in a row.

blocks.text: Scams that target freelancers
Wherever people look for work online, scammers follow. Learn the patterns so you can say no quickly.

blocks.title: Red flags: stop and check
items: Asks you to pay first
Overpays, then wants refund
Moves chat off platform fast
Huge pay for little work
Asks for codes or passwords
Unpaid big test task
blocks.caption: If any of these appear, pause, verify the client independently, and do not send money or codes.

items: **Pay to work:** a "client" asks you to pay for training, software or a registration fee before you can start. Real clients pay you, not the other way round.
**Overpayment refund:** someone sends more than agreed, by cheque or a transfer that later reverses, then begs you to refund the extra. The original payment disappears and your refund is gone.
**Account takeover:** someone asks for the six-digit code sent to your phone. That code lets them take over your WhatsApp or bank account. Never share it.
**Free work disguised as a test:** a short sample is normal. Writing ten full articles or designing a full brand "as a test" is unpaid work.

blocks.title: Protect client data too
blocks.text: Clients may share customer lists, passwords or private documents. Keep them only as long as needed, do not forward them, and use the client's own shared folders where possible. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for handling personal data, and careful handling also protects your reputation.

takeaways: Check your device, backup connection and accounts before taking clients.
Use traceable payment channels and confirm money in your own app.
Build a buffer for your real income gap, starting from your first earnings.
Never pay to work, refund overpayments, or share verification codes.

activity.title: Complete your readiness check
steps: Set up or tidy a professional email address and switch on two-step verification.
Create a WhatsApp Business profile with your offer line and working hours.
Choose your payment channel for local clients and, if relevant, for international clients.
List your essential monthly costs and calculate your buffer target for your real income gap.
Write the six scam red flags on a card or phone note you can check quickly.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your business profile, your buffer calculation, and your red-flag note.

quiz.q: Amaka can work 30 hours a week and spends 9 hours a week on finding clients, admin and unpaid calls. About how many billable hours does she have in a 4-week month?
quiz.explain: 30 minus 9 leaves 21 billable hours a week. 21 x 4 = 84 hours a month.

quiz.q: Which offer line is the strongest?
options: I help bakeries in Abuja get more orders by designing a monthly set of Instagram posts.
Social media, design, typing and editing at affordable rates.
I can do anything with computers.
I am a hardworking and creative writer.
quiz.explain: It names a specific client, a result they want, and a clear service, which makes it easy to understand and to price.

quiz.q: Hauwa finds many sellers on Fiverr already offering the service she wants to sell. What does this usually tell her?
options: People do buy this service, so she should be more specific to stand out.
She should lower her price to the cheapest on the site.
quiz.explain: Many sellers usually means real demand. The answer is a sharper niche and offer, not giving up or racing to the bottom on price.

quiz.q: A new client sends 150,000 naira for a 100,000 naira job, then asks you to refund the extra 50,000 urgently. What should you do?
options: Refund immediately to keep the client happy.
Do not refund until your own bank confirms the full payment has cleared and cannot be reversed, and treat it as a likely scam.
quiz.explain: The overpayment refund is a classic scam. The original payment often reverses, leaving you to lose the refund.

quiz.q: Chioma's essential costs are 180,000 naira a month and her current job covers 120,000. Using the three-month rule for her real gap, what buffer does she need?
quiz.explain: Her gap is 180,000 minus 120,000 = 60,000 a month. Three months of the gap is 60,000 x 3 = 180,000 naira.

quiz.q: According to the skill and demand matrix, what should you do with a skill you are strong at but for which you find almost no paying demand?
options: Keep it as a hobby, not the base of your income plan.
quiz.explain: Strong skill but low demand sits in the bottom-right box: enjoy it, but do not build your first income plan on it.

modules.title: Guided practice: packaging, pricing and winning first clients
modules.overview: Turn your service into clear packages with prices you can defend, reach the right clients with short personal pitches, and agree every job in writing before you start.

lessons.title: Packaging your service and calculating your minimum rate
objectives: Calculate a minimum hourly rate from your income target, costs and billable hours
Turn an hourly rate into a fixed package price
Design three clear packages with deliverables, revisions and turnaround
Account for platform and transfer fees when quoting

blocks.text: Clients rarely want to buy "hours". They want a finished result: 20 product descriptions, a month of posts, a translated survey. A **package** is a fixed bundle of work with a clear price, so the client knows exactly what they get and you know exactly what to do. Behind every package price, though, you need a number only you see: your **minimum hourly rate**, the lowest amount per working hour that keeps your business alive.
Your minimum rate in three steps

blocks.title: From income target to package price
items: Monthly income target
Add business costs
Divide by billable hours
Minimum hourly rate
Hours per job x rate
blocks.caption: Your package price starts from what you need to earn, not from the cheapest price you have seen online.

items: Decide your monthly **income target**: what you want to take home from freelancing each month.
Add your monthly **business costs**: data, electricity or fuel for power, software subscriptions, saving towards a new laptop or phone, and money you set aside for tax.
Divide the total by your **billable hours** per month, from Module 1. The answer is your minimum hourly rate.

blocks.title: Worked example: Amaka's minimum rate and package price
blocks.context: For example, Amaka writes product descriptions for small online shops. She has 72 billable hours a month (from Module 1). All naira figures are approximate.
steps: Income target: 250,000 naira a month.
Business costs: data 15,000, power and fuel 15,000, saving for a laptop 10,000. Total costs: 40,000 naira.
Total needed: 250,000 + 40,000 = 290,000 naira.
Minimum hourly rate: 290,000 / 72 = about 4,028 naira. She rounds up to 4,100 naira an hour.
She times herself: 20 product descriptions take about 6 hours to write plus 2 hours for checks and one revision round, so 8 hours.
Package cost to her: 8 x 4,100 = 32,800 naira. She prices the package at 35,000 naira.
blocks.result: Amaka now knows that any offer below about 33,000 naira for 20 descriptions loses her money in time. She can still choose to discount for a portfolio client, but she will do it knowingly.

blocks.title: Time yourself honestly
blocks.text: Do one practice job and record every minute: reading the brief, research, the work itself, checking, and messaging. Beginners nearly always underestimate the time, especially the messaging.
Three packages: basic, standard, premium
Offering three sizes helps the client choose how much to buy instead of deciding whether to buy at all. Each package lists the same things so they are easy to compare.

head: Package
What is included
Revisions
Delivery time
Price (approximate)
rows: 10 product descriptions, up to 80 words each
20 product descriptions, up to 100 words each
30 descriptions plus a short shop "About us" text

blocks.text: Check every package against your minimum rate. Basic: about 4 hours x 4,100 = 16,400 naira, so 18,000 is safe. Premium: about 13 hours x 4,100 = 53,300 naira, so 55,000 is safe. Many clients pick the middle package, so make that the one you most want to sell.

blocks.name: business-plan
blocks.alt: A woman standing beside a large plan on a board
blocks.caption: A package turns your skill into a clear plan the client can say yes to.

blocks.text: Define what is not included

Each package should also say what is outside it, for example "product photography not included" or "posting to the shop website is extra". This protects you later when a client asks for "one small thing" that is really a new job. You will use this in the written agreement two lessons from now.
Fees and international clients

If you work through a freelance platform, it keeps a service fee from what the client pays, and moving money to your bank can cost a withdrawal or exchange fee. These change over time, so always read the platform's current fee page before you set prices. Then quote high enough that **what reaches your account** still covers your minimum rate.

blocks.title: Worked example: allowing for fees
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa is quoted on a platform that, in this illustration, keeps 10 percent of each payment. She wants at least 90 US dollars to reach her account for a translation job.
steps: If she quotes 90 dollars, she receives 90 x 0.90 = 81 dollars. Too low.
To receive 90 dollars after a 10 percent fee, she divides: 90 / 0.90 = 100 dollars.
She also checks the withdrawal cost and exchange rate before converting to naira.
blocks.result: Hauwa quotes 100 dollars. She works out fees by dividing, not by adding 10 percent, because 90 + 9 = 99 would still leave her short.

blocks.text: Quote international clients in their own currency, usually US dollars, pounds or euros, and do not simply convert your naira price. Look at what freelancers with similar experience charge on the same platform, then check that your price still meets your minimum rate after fees.

takeaways: Minimum hourly rate = (income target + business costs) / billable hours.
Package price = estimated hours x minimum rate, rounded up.
Three packages with the same headings make choosing easy for the client.
To cover a platform fee, divide by what you keep, not add the fee on top.

activity.title: Build your price sheet
steps: Write your monthly income target and list your monthly business costs.
Calculate your minimum hourly rate using your billable hours from Module 1.
Do one timed practice job for your service and record total minutes.
Design Basic, Standard and Premium packages with deliverables, revisions, delivery time and price.
Write two things that are not included in any package.
activity.evidence: Your rate calculation and a one-page price sheet showing three packages and the exclusions.

lessons.title: Finding clients: outreach channels, pitch messages and follow-up
objectives: Choose two outreach channels that match your service and clients
Write a short, personal pitch with a clear next step
Follow up politely without becoming a nuisance
Track an outreach funnel and calculate your conversion rates

blocks.text: Clients do not find new freelancers by accident. Someone has to start the conversation, and at the beginning that someone is you. **Outreach** means contacting potential clients directly with a reason to talk. The goal of one message is not to close a sale. It is to get a reply.
Where to look

head: Channel
Best for
Watch out for
rows: Your warm network (friends, church, alumni, former colleagues)
First one to three clients and referrals
Friends expecting free work; agree price up front
Direct messages to local businesses (Instagram, WhatsApp, visits)
Be brief and specific; do not spam
Writing, virtual assistance, translation, NGO and corporate clients
Needs a complete profile before you message
Freelance platforms such as Upwork and Fiverr
International clients and steady job posts
Competition and fees; Upwork proposals use paid credits called Connects

blocks.text: Choose **two channels** and use them steadily for a month rather than trying all of them for a week. Your warm network is usually the fastest first channel, because people already trust you.

Before you message anyone, make sure the place they will check next looks ready. A business owner who likes your message will tap your WhatsApp Business profile, Instagram page or LinkedIn profile. It should show your offer line, one or two samples and how to contact you. On platforms, complete every profile section and write a headline that matches your offer line. When you reply to a job post, answer the client's actual problem in your first two lines, because that is often all they read in the list of proposals.
The four-part pitch

items: **Notice something specific** about their business: "I saw your Instagram has great cake photos but no prices in the captions."
**Offer one clear service** linked to it, using your offer line.
**Show proof**: one link or one image of a sample, not your whole life story.
**Ask for a small next step**: "Can I send you three sample captions for free this week?" or "Would a 10-minute call on Thursday work?"

blocks.title: Worked example: a pitch to a bakery
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Enugu offers Instagram caption writing and sees a home bakery whose posts have photos but no prices or ordering steps.
steps: Message: "Good afternoon, Mrs Ada. I love the red velvet cakes on your page. I noticed most posts do not say the price or how to order, which can make customers scroll past."
"I write short Instagram captions for home bakers that include the price, size and a simple order step."
"Here is a sample I wrote for a cake shop in Nsukka: [link]."
"Would you like me to rewrite three of your recent captions so you can see the difference? No cost for those three."
blocks.result: The message is under 90 words, personal, and asks for a tiny yes. Three free captions take Ifeoma about 30 minutes and show her skill far better than a long CV would.

blocks.title: Free samples have limits
blocks.text: A small sample of two or three items is reasonable when you are new. Do not give away whole projects. Decide in advance the maximum time you will spend on any free sample, for example 30 to 45 minutes.
Follow up, then stop

Busy people miss messages. A polite follow-up often gets more replies than the first message. A simple rhythm: send the pitch, follow up after 3 or 4 days with one short line, and send a final note about a week later. Then stop and move on. Never send messages late at night, and respect any "no, thank you" immediately.
Track your funnel
Your outreach works like a funnel: many messages lead to fewer replies, fewer calls, and a few paying clients. Tracking the numbers shows you exactly where to improve.

blocks.title: Outreach funnel
items: Paying clients
Calls or detailed chats
Replies
Messages sent
blocks.caption: Each level is smaller than the one below it; the percentages between levels tell you which step to improve.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a month of outreach numbers
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma tracks her first month in a Google Sheet.
steps: Messages sent: 40. Replies: 10. Reply rate: 10 / 40 = 25 percent.
Calls or detailed chats: 4. Reply-to-call rate: 4 / 10 = 40 percent.
Paying clients: 1. Call-to-client rate: 1 / 4 = 25 percent.
Overall: 1 client from 40 messages, or 2.5 percent.
She sees replies are healthy, but only 1 in 4 calls becomes a client, so she will improve how she runs calls and presents packages.
blocks.result: With these numbers, Ifeoma knows that to win 3 clients next month at the same rates she would need about 3 / 0.025 = 120 messages, or she can improve the weak step and need fewer.

blocks.name: message-sent
blocks.alt: A person sending a message from a phone
blocks.caption: Each short, personal message is one entry at the top of your funnel.

blocks.title: Do not buy contact lists or mass-message
blocks.text: Sending the same message to hundreds of strangers, or adding people to WhatsApp broadcast lists without permission, gets accounts reported and blocked, and it damages your reputation. Personal messages to well-chosen businesses work better.

takeaways: Pick two outreach channels and use them consistently for a month.
A good pitch notices something, offers one service, shows proof and asks for a small step.
Follow up twice, politely, then move on.
Track messages, replies, calls and clients to find the weak step.

activity.title: Send your first ten pitches
steps: List ten specific potential clients from your two chosen channels.
Write a four-part pitch for each, with one personal observation per client.
Send the ten pitches over three days and log the date of each.
Follow up after 3 or 4 days with one short line.
Record replies and calls in a simple funnel table and calculate your reply rate.
activity.evidence: Your outreach log (client, channel, date sent, follow-up, outcome) and your calculated reply rate.

lessons.title: From enquiry to agreement: discovery calls, scope and written terms
objectives: Run a short discovery conversation using a set of key questions
Write a scope summary that lists deliverables, deadlines and exclusions
Include deposit, revision and ownership terms in a simple written agreement
Handle extra requests with a change request instead of free work

blocks.text: When a potential client replies "How much?" or "Let's talk", the job is not yet won. Many freelance disputes start right here, when both sides agree in a hurry and later remember the job differently. This lesson turns an interested enquiry into a clear, written agreement before you do any paid work.
The discovery conversation

A **discovery call** is a short conversation, 10 to 20 minutes by phone, WhatsApp call or Google Meet, where you find out what the client really needs. You talk less and ask more. Use these questions and write the answers down:

items: What do you need done, and what prompted it now?
Who is it for, and what should they do or feel after seeing it?
Do you have examples you like, or materials I should use (logo, photos, old documents)?
When do you need it, and is that date fixed?
Who gives the final approval?
What budget have you set aside for this?

blocks.title: Asking about budget is normal
blocks.text: Professionals ask about budget so they can suggest the right package. If the client does not know, describe your three packages and let them choose.
Write the scope

**Scope** means exactly what work is included. After the call, send a written scope summary the same day. A WhatsApp message or email is fine for small jobs; for bigger jobs use a short document. It should contain:

head: Item
Example wording
rows: 12 Instagram post designs (1080 x 1080 pixels) and captions for December
Logo, 15 product photos and price list by 3 December
Drafts by 6 December; final files by 9 December
Up to 2 rounds of changes on the drafts
Posting to the page, paid adverts, new photography
60,000 naira: 50 percent deposit before starting, 50 percent before final files
Client may use the final designs freely once paid in full; freelancer may show them in her portfolio unless the client asks otherwise

blocks.text: End with a direct question: "If this is correct, please reply 'Agreed' and send the deposit, and I will start." A clear "Agreed" in writing is your record of the deal.

blocks.title: From enquiry to start
items: Enquiry
Discovery call
Written scope sent
Client agrees
Deposit confirmed
Work starts
blocks.caption: Paid work begins only after the scope is agreed in writing and the deposit has arrived.

blocks.name: contract-signed
blocks.alt: Two people agreeing a signed document
blocks.caption: A short written agreement protects both you and the client.

blocks.text: Deposits and payment terms

A **deposit** is part payment before you start. It shows the client is serious and protects you if they disappear. Many freelancers ask for 50 percent up front for new clients, with the balance before final files are released. For larger projects you can split payment into milestones, for example 40 percent, 30 percent and 30 percent. For international platform jobs, use the platform's own payment protection, such as funded milestones, rather than moving the payment outside the platform.

blocks.title: Worked example: handling an extra request
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Abuja agreed to design 12 posts for 60,000 naira, about 5,000 naira per post. On day 4 the client asks her to "also make a quick flyer for the Christmas promo and 3 more posts".
steps: She checks the scope: the flyer and 3 extra posts are not included.
She replies warmly: "Happy to help with these. They are outside our current scope, so here is a quick change request."
Extra posts: 3 x 5,000 = 15,000 naira. Flyer: her design rate for a flyer is 12,000 naira. Total change: 27,000 naira.
She adds one extra day to the deadline because of the added work and asks for the change to be paid with the final balance.
blocks.result: The client agrees in writing. The new total is 60,000 + 27,000 = 87,000 naira, and the extra work is paid instead of quietly absorbed.

blocks.text: When the client hesitates

Some clients agree on the call, then go quiet when the deposit is mentioned. Send one friendly reminder after two or three days: "Just checking whether you would like to go ahead with the December posts. I am holding a slot for you until Friday." If they say the price is too high, offer a smaller package instead of cutting the price of the same work. For example, offer 8 posts instead of 12 rather than 12 posts for less money. If there is still no answer after your reminder, release the slot and move on without bitterness. Many quiet clients come back months later.

blocks.title: Scope creep
blocks.text: **Scope creep** is when a job slowly grows through many "small" extra requests. It is the main reason freelancers end up working for very little per hour. Answer every extra request kindly, then price it.

If you also write formal proposals for larger clients, the WODDI Institute course on proposal writing covers full business proposals. For most small freelance jobs, a clear scope message like the one above is enough.

takeaways: Ask questions first; write the answers down.
Send a written scope with deliverables, deadline, revisions, exclusions and payment.
Start paid work only after written agreement and a confirmed deposit.
Price every extra request with a change request.

activity.title: Create your scope template
steps: Copy the seven scope items into a WhatsApp note or Google Doc template.
Fill it in for a realistic job in your service, using your package prices.
Write your six discovery questions where you can see them during calls.
Write a short, friendly change request message you can reuse.
Role-play a discovery call with a friend and fill in the template from it.
activity.evidence: Your completed scope template for one realistic job and your saved change request message.

quiz.q: Ngozi wants to take home 200,000 naira a month, has 40,000 naira of monthly business costs and 60 billable hours a month. What is her minimum hourly rate?
A platform keeps 20 percent of each payment. Hauwa needs 80 dollars to reach her. What should she quote?
quiz.explain: She keeps 80 percent, so she divides: 80 / 0.80 = 100 dollars. Adding 20 percent (96 dollars) would leave her with only 76.80.

quiz.q: Which pitch opening is strongest?
options: Dear Sir/Madam, I am a hardworking freelancer looking for work.
I saw your menu photos are lovely but the prices are hard to read on a phone.
Do you need any help with anything?
quiz.explain: A specific observation about their business shows you paid attention and links straight to the problem your service solves.

quiz.q: Ifeoma sent 50 messages, got 15 replies, had 5 calls and won 1 client. Which step most needs improving?
quiz.explain: Replies are 30 percent and calls are a third of replies, but only 1 in 5 calls became a client, so the call and offer stage is weakest.

quiz.q: Halfway through a 12-post job, the client asks for 4 extra posts. What is the best response?
options: Agree kindly, then send a written change request with the extra price and any new deadline.
Stop the job until the client apologises.
Do them free to keep the client happy.
quiz.explain: A friendly change request keeps the relationship and makes sure extra work is paid.

quiz.q: When should paid work start on a new client project?
options: After the discovery call, even without a deposit
As soon as the client says "let's talk"
After the scope is agreed in writing and the deposit is confirmed in your account
After the final files are sent
quiz.explain: Written agreement plus a confirmed deposit protects you from misunderstandings and disappearing clients.

modules.title: Quality and evidence: delivering, getting paid and tracking your numbers
modules.overview: Deliver work on time with clear communication, invoice properly and collect what you are owed, act ethically with client information, and use a few simple numbers to see whether your freelancing is really working.

lessons.title: Delivering on time: project workflow, updates and handover
objectives: Plan a project backwards from the deadline with a safety margin
Check work against the agreed scope before sending it
Send clear progress updates and give bad news early
Hand over final files in a tidy, usable form

blocks.text: Clients come back to freelancers who are **reliable**, not only talented. In practice, reliable means three things: you deliver what was agreed, you deliver when you said, and the client never has to chase you for news. This lesson gives you a simple workflow that makes all three normal.
The delivery workflow

blocks.title: Five-stage delivery workflow
items: Kick-off and materials
Plan backwards with buffer
Draft and self-check
Revisions as agreed
Final handover
blocks.caption: Following the same five stages on every job makes your quality steady, even on busy weeks.

items: **Kick-off:** confirm the scope, collect every material the client promised (logo, photos, documents) and say when the first draft will arrive.
**Plan backwards:** put the client deadline in your calendar, then set your own earlier deadline with a buffer for power cuts, data problems or illness.
**Draft and self-check:** do the work, then check it line by line against the written scope before the client sees it.
**Revisions:** collect all the client's changes in one message per round, make them, and confirm when a round is finished.
**Handover:** send final files with clear names, in the right format, with a short note on how to use them.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning backwards with a buffer
blocks.context: For example, Zainab agrees to deliver 12 social media designs in 7 working days. She works about 4 billable hours a day.
steps: She estimates 12 hours of design and 3 hours for one revision round: 15 hours in total.
She adds a buffer of about 20 percent: 15 x 1.2 = 18 hours, or 4 and a half working days at 4 hours a day.
She has 7 working days, so she sets her own target to send final files on day 6, one day before the client deadline.
She schedules: drafts sent on day 3, client feedback by the end of day 4, revisions on day 5, final checks and handover on day 6.
She tells the client: "You will receive drafts on day 3. Please send all changes in one message by the evening of day 4 so I can finish on time."
blocks.result: Zainab delivers a day early even after a power cut on day 5 costs her 3 hours, because the buffer absorbed it.

blocks.title: Ask for feedback in one message
blocks.text: Ask clients to collect all their changes into one message per revision round. Scattered voice notes over several days are the fastest way to miss a change and blow a deadline.
The self-check before anything is sent

Put the written scope next to your work and tick each item. Then add checks for your service. A writer reads the text aloud once and runs a spelling check, then confirms every name, price and phone number against the client's materials. A designer checks the size in pixels, the spelling on every design, and that the client's logo and colours are correct. A virtual assistant checks that every calendar entry has the right date and time zone. Errors in names, prices and phone numbers are the ones clients notice first and forgive least.
Communication that builds trust

Agree how and when you will communicate: WhatsApp for quick questions, email for files and approvals, and your working hours. A simple rule many freelancers use is to reply to client messages within one working day, even if the reply is only "Received, I will send the answer by 3 pm tomorrow."

If something will be late, say so **as soon as you know**, not on the deadline day. Give the reason in one line, a new date, and what the client will receive in the meantime. Clients forgive an early warning far more easily than a silent delay.

head: Situation
What to send
rows: Confirmation of materials received and the date of the first draft
A short progress update, ideally with a preview
The problem, your solution and any new date, sent the same day
Files, a short summary of what was done, and how to request any agreed revisions

blocks.text: Working across time zones

Nigeria uses West Africa Time, one hour ahead of Greenwich Mean Time. The UK is one hour behind Nigeria in winter and on the same time in summer. New York is five or six hours behind, depending on the season. When you agree a deadline with an international client, write the time zone, for example "Friday 5 pm WAT", so nobody is confused.
A clean handover

items: Name files clearly: ClientName_Project_Final_v2.pdf, not IMG_2045.
Send the format the client needs: PNG or JPG for posts, PDF for print, editable DOCX or Google Docs for text they will change.
Share via a Google Drive folder and check the link opens for "anyone with the link" or for the client's email.
Keep a backup copy for an agreed time, for example 3 months, then delete files containing private client information.

blocks.name: work-in-progress
blocks.alt: A woman arranging project cards on a board
blocks.caption: Breaking a job into stages and dates keeps your work moving and your promises realistic.

takeaways: Plan backwards from the deadline and add a buffer of about 20 percent.
Check every piece against the written scope before the client sees it.
Give bad news early, with a solution and a new date.
Hand over clearly named files in the format the client needs.

activity.title: Plan one job end to end
steps: Take a realistic job for your service and estimate its hours, including one revision round.
Add a 20 percent buffer and plan backwards from a client deadline in your calendar.
Write your kick-off message and your final delivery message as templates.
Create a Google Drive folder structure you will reuse for every client.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your calendar plan with your own early deadline, plus your two message templates.

lessons.title: Invoices, late payments and ethical practice
objectives: Prepare a complete invoice with correct totals and balance due
Follow a polite, firm sequence for chasing late payments
Apply honest practice on capacity, confidentiality and use of AI tools
Keep records you can use for tax and planning

blocks.text: You have done good work. Now it must become money in your account. An **invoice** is a formal request for payment that lists what you did and what is owed. It looks professional, it makes it easy for a business to pay you, and it becomes part of your records. Send one for every job, even for friends.
What every invoice shows

blocks.title: Invoice checklist
items: Your name and contacts
Client name and invoice number
Date and due date
Itemised work and amounts
Deposit paid and balance due
How to pay you
blocks.caption: If any one of these is missing, payment is more likely to be delayed or disputed.

blocks.text: You can make invoices with a free template in Google Docs or Google Sheets, or with free invoicing apps. Number them in order, for example INV-2026-001, INV-2026-002, so you can find them later. Use the same name and bank account name on every invoice to avoid confusion.

blocks.title: Worked example: an invoice with a change request
blocks.context: For example, Zainab's December job was agreed at 60,000 naira with a 50 percent deposit, then a change request added 27,000 naira.
steps: Line 1: 12 Instagram post designs and captions, 60,000 naira.
Line 2: change request: 3 extra posts at 5,000 naira each, 15,000 naira.
Line 3: change request: Christmas promo flyer, 12,000 naira.
Less deposit received on 1 December: 30,000 naira (50 percent of 60,000).
Balance due: 87,000 minus 30,000 = 57,000 naira, due before final files are released, payable to her named business account.
blocks.result: The client sees exactly how 57,000 naira was reached, so there is nothing to argue about and payment arrives the same day.

blocks.name: printing-invoices
blocks.alt: A woman printing invoices beside a computer
blocks.caption: A clear, numbered invoice turns finished work into money and records.

blocks.text: When payment is late
Most late payments are disorganisation, not bad faith. A calm, regular sequence works best. Keep every reminder short and polite, and always attach or link the invoice again.

head: When
Message
rows: Friendly reminder: "Hello, a quick reminder that invoice INV-2026-014 for 57,000 naira is due today. Thank you."
Second reminder asking if there is any problem with the invoice
Firmer note: further work and final files are on hold until payment, as agreed
A phone call; for large sums, ask a trusted adviser about your options

blocks.title: Keep leverage
blocks.text: This is why the deposit and "final files after full payment" terms matter. Send watermarked or low-resolution previews for approval, and release final, full-quality files after the balance is paid.
Ethical freelancing

items: **Capacity:** only accept work you can deliver well on time. Saying "I can start on the 15th" is better than accepting and failing.
**Honesty about skill:** do not claim experience you do not have. Say "I have done this for two clients" rather than "I am an expert".
**Confidentiality:** do not share client documents, customer lists or private messages, and do not post client work publicly without permission.
**Original work:** do not copy other people's writing or designs; use properly licensed fonts, images and music.
**AI tools:** if you use AI to draft or design, check every fact and word yourself, follow the client's rules, and be honest if they ask how the work was made.

blocks.text: When a client is unhappy

Sometimes a client says the work is not what they wanted. Stay calm and go back to the written scope together. If you missed something that was agreed, fix it quickly and without extra charge. If the client now wants something different from what was agreed, explain kindly that this is a change and offer a price for it. If you truly cannot satisfy a client, a partial refund of the unfinished part can be a fair way to close the job, and it protects your reputation. Never argue in public comments or reviews.

blocks.title: Do not move platform clients off the platform
blocks.text: If you met a client on a freelance platform, taking payment outside it usually breaks the platform's terms and removes its payment protection. Your account can be closed and you lose the protection if the client does not pay.
Records and tax

Freelance income is taxable personal income in Nigeria. For self-employed people, personal income tax is handled by the internal revenue service of the state where you live, and you may need a Tax Identification Number (TIN). Rules change, so ask your state revenue service or a qualified tax adviser what applies to you. Whatever the rules, keep every invoice, payment confirmation and business expense receipt in one folder by month. Good records make tax, loans and planning much easier.

Some freelancers move a fixed share of every payment into a separate savings pocket for tax and business costs as soon as it arrives. The exact share is a personal decision, but the habit stops you spending money that is not really yours to spend.

takeaways: Send a numbered, itemised invoice for every job, showing deposit and balance.
Chase late payments on a calm, fixed schedule and keep final files until paid.
Ethical freelancing means honesty on capacity and skill, and protecting client information.
Keep invoices and receipts by month; ask your state revenue service about tax.

activity.title: Set up your invoice and records system
steps: Create an invoice template in Google Docs or Sheets with all six checklist items.
Fill in a practice invoice for a job with a deposit and one change request, and check the arithmetic.
Save your three payment reminder messages as quick replies or notes.
Create a records folder with one sub-folder per month for invoices and receipts.
activity.evidence: Your completed practice invoice and a screenshot of your records folder and saved reminders.

lessons.title: The numbers that matter: income, effective rate and repeat clients
objectives: Keep a simple monthly freelance tracker in a spreadsheet
Calculate your effective hourly rate and compare it with your minimum rate
Measure repeat clients and average job value
Use a monthly review to decide one change for next month

blocks.text: Being busy and being profitable are not the same thing. You can work every day, answer messages until midnight, and still earn less per hour than you planned. A few numbers, checked once a month, tell you the truth and show you what to change.
Your freelance tracker
Create a Google Sheet with one row per job. Keep it simple enough that you will actually update it.
On a second tab, record your **total** working hours each week, including outreach, calls, admin and learning. Your phone's timer or a paper notebook is enough.
Effective hourly rate

Your **effective hourly rate** is what you really earned for every hour you worked on your freelance business: money received divided by all working hours, billable and non-billable. Compare it with the minimum rate you calculated in Module 2.

blocks.title: Worked example: a busy month that paid too little
blocks.context: For example, Amaka's minimum rate is 4,100 naira an hour. In March she received payment for five jobs.
steps: Billable hours on those jobs: 60. Rate on billable hours: 180,000 / 60 = 3,000 naira.
Non-billable hours (outreach, calls, admin): 30. Total hours: 90.
Effective hourly rate: 180,000 / 90 = 2,000 naira, less than half her minimum rate.
Looking at her tracker, two jobs ran over their estimated hours because of unplanned revision rounds, and she spent 12 hours on free samples.
blocks.result: Amaka decides on two changes for April: a firm limit of 2 revision rounds stated in every scope, and a maximum of 30 minutes per free sample.

blocks.text: Three more useful numbers

items: **Average job value:** total money received divided by number of jobs. 180,000 / 5 = 36,000 naira. Raising this, for example by selling the Standard package more often, is often easier than finding more clients.
**Repeat client rate:** clients who came back divided by total clients. If 2 of 5 clients in a quarter were returning clients, that is 2 / 5 = 40 percent. Repeat clients cost far less time to win.
**Outreach conversion:** paying clients divided by messages sent, from your funnel in Module 2.

blocks.title: Look at trends, not one month
blocks.text: Freelance income goes up and down. Compare each number with the previous two or three months before drawing conclusions. One slow month does not mean you have failed.
Turning numbers into targets

Your numbers also tell you how much work you need. Divide your monthly money target by your average job value to see how many jobs you need. Then use your outreach conversion to see how many messages that takes. If the answer is unrealistic, the fix is usually to raise the value of each job or win more repeat work, not to send hundreds more messages.

blocks.title: Worked example: how many jobs and messages?
blocks.context: For example, Amaka needs 290,000 naira a month (her income target plus business costs from Module 2). Her average job value is 36,000 naira and 1 in 40 outreach messages becomes a client.
steps: Jobs needed: 290,000 / 36,000 = about 8.1, so 9 jobs a month.
If every job came from cold outreach: 9 x 40 = 360 messages a month, which is not realistic alongside the work itself.
If 4 of the 9 jobs are repeat clients, she needs only 5 new clients: 5 x 40 = 200 messages. Still heavy.
If she also lifts her average job value to 50,000 naira by promoting Premium and monthly packages: 290,000 / 50,000 = 5.8, so 6 jobs.
With 3 of those 6 from repeat clients, she needs 3 new clients: 3 x 40 = 120 messages a month, about 6 a working day.
blocks.result: Amaka sees that repeat work and bigger packages, not more messages alone, make her target reachable. These become the focus of Module 4.

head: If this number is low
Try this first
rows: Limit revision rounds and free samples; raise package prices for new clients
Promote the Standard and Premium packages; offer a monthly package
Ask for feedback and offer a next piece of work at every handover
Make pitches more specific; improve your samples and discovery calls

blocks.text: The monthly review

blocks.title: Monthly review cycle
items: Update tracker
Calculate key numbers
Compare with targets
Choose one change
Test it for a month
blocks.caption: Changing one thing at a time shows you clearly what made the difference.

blocks.text: Set a fixed date, for example the last Saturday of each month, and spend 30 minutes on the review. Write your four numbers (money received, effective hourly rate, average job value, repeat client rate) at the top of a page. Then answer three questions: What worked? What cost me time without paying? What one change will I test next month?

blocks.name: growth-analytics
blocks.alt: A woman looking at a rising chart on a screen
blocks.caption: A monthly look at four numbers shows whether your freelancing is growing in the right way.

blocks.title: Separate business money
blocks.text: If you can, receive freelance payments into one account or wallet used only for the business. It makes your tracker much easier to check against your bank statement.

takeaways: Track every job and all your working hours, not just paid ones.
Effective hourly rate = money received / total hours worked.
Average job value and repeat client rate often matter more than more clients.
Review monthly and test one change at a time.

activity.title: Build and test your tracker
steps: Create a Google Sheet with the seven job columns and a weekly hours tab.
Enter your practice or real jobs from this course so far.
Calculate effective hourly rate, average job value and repeat client rate using sheet formulas.
Write the one change you would make next month based on the numbers.

quiz.q: Zainab must deliver work that needs about 20 hours. Using a 20 percent buffer, how many hours should she plan?
quiz.explain: 20 x 1.2 = 24 hours. The buffer protects the deadline from power cuts, illness and extra feedback.

quiz.q: An international client in New York asks for files "by 5 pm Friday". What should you do?
options: Confirm the time zone in writing, for example 5 pm New York time or the WAT equivalent.
Ignore the time and send whenever ready.
quiz.explain: New York is several hours behind Nigeria, so writing the time zone avoids missing or misreading the deadline.

quiz.q: A job total is 90,000 naira, including a change request. The client paid a 40,000 naira deposit. What is the balance due on the invoice?
quiz.explain: 90,000 minus 40,000 = 50,000 naira balance due.

quiz.q: An invoice is 7 days overdue after two polite reminders. What is the recommended next step?
options: Post the client's name on social media.
Send a firmer note that further work and final files are on hold until payment, as agreed.
quiz.explain: A firm, polite note backed by your written terms keeps it professional and keeps your leverage.

quiz.q: In a month Amaka received 120,000 naira and worked 40 billable and 20 non-billable hours. What was her effective hourly rate?
quiz.explain: Effective rate uses all hours: 120,000 / (40 + 20) = 120,000 / 60 = 2,000 naira.

quiz.q: A client you met on a freelance platform asks to pay you directly by bank transfer to "save fees". What is the safest response?
options: Keep payment on the platform, as moving it usually breaks the terms and removes payment protection.
Ask the client to pay double.
quiz.explain: Taking payment off-platform can get your account closed and leaves you without protection if the client does not pay.

modules.title: Portfolio and impact: reputation, repeat work and your 90-day plan
modules.overview: Turn finished jobs into testimonials, referrals and repeat clients, explain your value with confidence in price conversations, and complete your Freelance Launch Project with a realistic 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Turning finished jobs into testimonials, referrals and repeat work
objectives: Ask for specific feedback and a usable testimonial at the end of each job
Write a three-line case snapshot from a finished job
Ask satisfied clients for referrals in a natural way
Offer a next piece of work at every handover

blocks.text: Your first clients are hard to win because strangers have no proof that you are good. Every finished job is a chance to create that proof. Freelancers who grow steadily do the same few things at the end of every job: they ask for feedback, collect a testimonial, record what they achieved, and offer the next piece of work. This lesson turns those into habits.
The reputation loop

blocks.title: From one job to the next client
items: Deliver well
Ask for feedback
Get a testimonial
Share the proof
Receive referrals
blocks.caption: Each step makes the next client easier to win, so your outreach effort falls over time.

blocks.text: Asking for feedback and a testimonial
Ask within a few days of handover, while the client is still pleased. General questions get general answers like "Good job, thanks." Specific questions get answers you can learn from and quote.

items: What was the main problem before you hired me?
What difference has the work made so far?
What did you find easy or helpful about working with me?
What one thing could I do better next time?
May I quote your answer, with your first name and business name, on my profiles?

head: Weak testimonial
Strong testimonial
rows: "Before Ifeoma, our cake posts had no prices and people kept asking in DMs. Now every caption has the price and how to order, and we spend less time answering the same question." Ada, Ada's Cakes, Enugu
"Hauwa translated our 40-question survey into Hausa in four days, and the field team said respondents understood it easily." Programme officer, health NGO, Kano

blocks.text: A strong testimonial names the problem, the work and a result, and says who it is from. Always ask permission before you publish it, and never write a testimonial yourself and put a client's name on it.

blocks.title: Worked example: a feedback request and what came from it
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma finished a month of captions for Ada's Cakes. Four days later she sends a WhatsApp message.
steps: "Good morning, Mrs Ada. I hope the new captions are working well. Could you answer three quick questions to help me improve? 1) What was the main problem before? 2) What has changed since? 3) What could I do better?"
Ada replies with a voice note. Ifeoma types up the key sentences and sends them back: "May I use these words, with your name and business, on my page?"
Ada agrees and adds: "Customers now ask fewer questions before ordering." Her one improvement: send drafts earlier in the week.
Ifeoma adds a three-line case snapshot to her WhatsApp catalogue and LinkedIn Featured section.
blocks.result: One short message gave Ifeoma a quotable testimonial, a real improvement point, and a case snapshot she can send with every pitch.

blocks.text: The three-line case snapshot

A **case snapshot** is a very short story of one job: **Problem:** posts had no prices and customers kept asking in DMs. **Work:** wrote 12 captions with price, size and order steps. **Result:** the owner reports fewer repeat questions before ordering. Use the client's own words for the result. Never invent numbers such as "sales doubled" unless the client gave them to you and agreed you can share them.

blocks.name: leave-a-review
blocks.alt: A person leaving a star review on a phone
blocks.caption: Specific, permitted reviews from real clients are your strongest proof.

blocks.text: Where to keep your proof

Keep all your proof in one Google Drive folder called "Proof", with sub-folders for testimonials, samples and case snapshots, so you can send the right item in seconds when a potential client asks. Then show your best two or three pieces where clients actually look: your WhatsApp Business catalogue, the Featured section of your LinkedIn profile, your platform profile, and your portfolio if you have one. If a client asked you to keep their work private, describe the job without naming them, for example "a health NGO in northern Nigeria", and do not show the documents themselves.
Referrals and repeat work

A **referral** is a client recommending you to someone else. Satisfied clients often know people with the same problem: other bakers, other NGOs, other coaches. Ask simply, once, after positive feedback: "I am glad it helped. If you know another business owner who could use this, I would be grateful if you shared my number."

At every handover, also suggest one logical next piece of work, for example next month's posts, the Hausa version of a second leaflet, or a quarterly bookkeeping tidy-up. Make it concrete, with a package name and price, so saying yes is easy.

blocks.title: Platform reviews
blocks.text: On platforms such as Upwork and Fiverr, reviews and ratings after each job strongly affect whether new clients see and trust you. Deliver to the agreed scope, communicate on the platform, and politely remind clients that a review helps you, without ever offering anything in exchange for a good one.

takeaways: Ask specific feedback questions within a few days of handover.
Strong testimonials name the problem, the work, a result and the person, with permission.
A three-line case snapshot is proof you can send with every pitch.
Ask once for referrals and always offer a concrete next piece of work.

Add it to your WhatsApp Business catalogue, LinkedIn or portfolio.

lessons.title: Explaining your value and handling price conversations
objectives: Describe your service in terms of outcomes, not just tasks
Give a clear 30-second explanation of what you do
Respond to "too expensive" by adjusting scope, not cutting your rate
Offer a monthly package and plan a fair rate increase

blocks.text: Clients do not buy captions, spreadsheets or translations for their own sake. They buy what those things do for them: more orders, fewer mistakes, time back, reaching people they could not reach before. When you describe your work in terms of these **outcomes**, your price makes sense to the client.

blocks.title: Task talk versus outcome talk
items: Task talk
Outcome talk
blocks.caption: Outcome talk connects your price to something the client already values.
right: Customers see price and order steps
You get back hours each week

blocks.text: Your 30-second explanation
People will ask "So what do you do?" at weddings, in church, in the market and on calls. Prepare a short answer in three parts and practise it aloud until it feels natural.

items: **Who and what:** your offer line. "I help home bakers get more orders by writing Instagram captions that include price and how to order."
**Proof:** one result. "One bakery in Enugu told me customers now ask fewer questions before ordering."
**Invitation:** a light next step. "If you know a baker who struggles with posting, I would love to help."

blocks.name: business-deal
blocks.alt: Two people shaking hands over a deal
blocks.caption: A clear explanation of value turns a casual chat into a client conversation.

blocks.text: Use the client's own numbers

The most convincing value statements use numbers the client already knows. Ask on the discovery call: "How many hours a week do you spend on this now?" or "How many customers ask the same question before ordering?" If a coach says she spends 6 hours a week on email and booking, and your service gives most of those hours back, she can judge for herself what that time is worth to her. You do not need to promise sales figures. You help the client see the cost of the problem they already have.

With international clients on platforms, the same idea applies in writing. Open your proposal with their problem in your own words, state the outcome you will deliver, and list exactly what is included. Clients reading many proposals quickly notice the one that shows it understood the job.
When a client says "too expensive"
Treat "too expensive" as a question, not a final no. Stay calm and find out what they are comparing you to. Then choose one of these responses:

items: **Reduce the scope, not the rate:** "For 35,000 naira I can do 20 descriptions. Within 18,000 I can do the 10 most important products first."
**Split the payment:** offer staged payments, for example half now and half on delivery, if cash flow is the real problem.
**Explain what is included:** revisions, research, quick turnaround, and your record of results.
**Let it go politely:** if the budget is far below your minimum rate, thank them and leave the door open. Not every client is your client.

blocks.title: Why not just give a discount?
blocks.text: Cutting the price for the same work teaches the client that your first price was not real, and it pushes you below your minimum rate. If you do discount, attach it to something real: a longer commitment, payment in full up front, or permission to use the job as a portfolio case.
Monthly packages

A **retainer** or monthly package is an agreement for the same service every month, for example 12 social posts or 10 hours of virtual assistance. It gives the client steady support and gives you predictable income with less selling. Agree the monthly scope, the payment date (usually at the start of the month), what happens to unused hours, and how either side can end it, for example with 30 days' notice.

blocks.title: Worked example: offering a monthly package
blocks.context: For example, Zainab's client paid 60,000 naira for 12 one-off posts that took her 15 hours. The client now asks for posts every month.
steps: One-off rate earned: 60,000 / 15 = 4,000 naira an hour.
Because she now knows the brand, she estimates each month will take 11 hours.
She offers a 3-month package at 55,000 naira a month, paid on the 1st, with 30 days' notice to end.
Her rate on the package: 55,000 / 11 = 5,000 naira an hour, higher than before even with the lower price.
Three months of income secured: 55,000 x 3 = 165,000 naira without new outreach.
blocks.result: The client pays less per month, and Zainab earns more per hour with steady income. Both sides gain because repeat work takes less time.

blocks.text: Raising your rates

As your skill, speed and proof grow, your prices should grow too. Raise prices for **new** clients first. For existing clients, give written notice, for example 30 days, and thank them for their support. A small, regular rise is easier for clients to accept than a big jump after years of the same price.

takeaways: Describe outcomes the client values, not only tasks you perform.
Practise a 30-second explanation: who and what, proof, invitation.
Answer "too expensive" by reducing scope or splitting payment, not cutting your rate.
Monthly packages and planned rate rises build steady, growing income.

lessons.title: Freelance Launch Project and your 90-day plan
objectives: Assemble your service description, sample and real outreach evidence
Report honest results, including no responses and refusals
Write a 90-day plan with weekly outreach targets and milestones
Check your evidence against the certificate checklist

blocks.text: This final lesson brings everything together into your **Freelance Launch Project**. The aim is not a perfect business. It is a real start: a clear service, proof you can do it, at least three genuine outreach attempts with honest results, and a realistic plan for the next 90 days.
What your launch pack contains

head: Part
What to include
From lesson
rows: Offer line, three packages with prices, what is not included
At least one sample or real job, with a three-line case snapshot
At least 3 real pitches, dates, follow-ups and honest outcomes
Weekly targets, milestones and a monthly review date

blocks.text: Report outreach results honestly. "Sent 12 pitches, 3 replies, 1 call, 0 clients yet" is a perfectly good result for a first attempt, and it tells you where to improve. Do not invent clients, payments or testimonials. Remove or blur private details such as phone numbers before you submit screenshots.

blocks.name: goals
blocks.alt: A woman reaching a target with a flag
blocks.caption: A 90-day plan turns your first outreach into steady, measurable progress.

blocks.text: Building a 90-day plan

Ninety days is long enough to see real results from steady outreach and short enough to stay focused. Split it into three 30-day phases, each with one main goal, weekly activity targets, and a number to check at the end.

blocks.title: 90 days in three phases
items: Days 1 to 30: first clients
Days 31 to 60: proof and process
Days 61 to 90: repeat and raise
blocks.caption: Each phase builds on the one before: clients first, then proof, then steadier and better-paid work.

blocks.title: Worked example: Hauwa's 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa offers Hausa to English and English to Hausa translation. She can give 15 hours a week. Her launch project produced 3 pitches, 1 reply and no paid job yet.
steps: Days 1 to 30: send 5 personal pitches a week to NGOs, researchers and media houses (20 in total), complete her LinkedIn profile, and win 1 to 2 first clients. Check: reply rate.
Days 31 to 60: keep 5 pitches a week, deliver every job with her scope and invoice templates, and collect 2 testimonials. Check: effective hourly rate against her minimum of 4,500 naira.
Days 61 to 90: offer a monthly or multi-document package to her best client, ask two happy clients for referrals, and raise her price for new clients by 10 percent. Check: repeat client rate.
Total planned pitches: 5 a week x about 13 weeks = 65 pitches.
At her current rate of 1 reply per 3 pitches, 65 pitches should bring 65 / 3 = about 21 or 22 replies, enough conversations to test and improve her calls.
blocks.result: Hauwa's plan is specific, measurable and fits her 15 hours a week. Her monthly review dates are fixed in her calendar for days 30, 60 and 90.

blocks.title: Plan for weeks that go wrong
blocks.text: Illness, family events and power cuts will happen. Build in one lighter week per month and decide in advance what the minimum is for a hard week, for example 2 pitches and one tracker update.
Common mistakes in 90-day plans

items: **Targets with no activity:** "earn 300,000 naira" without saying how many pitches or packages that needs.
**Too many channels:** trying five platforms at once instead of two used well.
**No review dates:** a plan nobody checks becomes a wish.
**Ignoring time:** planning 30 hours of work a week when you have 15.

blocks.text: Check your plan against these four mistakes before you submit it. Every target should connect to an action you can do this week, such as "5 pitches" or "1 testimonial request".
Certificate checklist

items: Offer line and three priced packages with exclusions.
Minimum hourly rate calculation.
At least one work sample with a case snapshot.
Evidence of at least 3 real outreach attempts with honest outcomes.
Scope template, invoice template and tracker.
90-day plan with weekly targets, three milestones and review dates.

blocks.text: Presenting your launch pack

Put everything in one Google Doc or one Drive folder with a short contents list at the top, so a reviewer can find each part in under a minute. Start with your offer line, then follow the order of the table above. Add a five-sentence reflection at the end: what went well, what surprised you, what a refusal or silence taught you, and the first change you will test in your 90-day plan.
Keep going after the course

Freelancing rewards consistency more than talent alone. The women who succeed are usually not the ones with the best first month, but the ones who keep pitching, keep improving one thing at a time, and treat every client as a future referral. Your skill was already yours. This course has given you the structure to sell it. Your monthly review will tell you what to change next.
If you want to go deeper on any part, the WODDI Institute courses on online portfolio building, proposal writing, and pricing and selling build directly on what you have done here.

takeaways: Your launch pack proves a real start: service, sample, outreach, tools and plan.
Honest results, including zero clients so far, are valid evidence.
Plan 90 days in three phases with weekly targets and a number to check.
Consistency and one change at a time build sustainable freelance income.
